newsitem.title: USA: Cities moving to ban tobacco billboards.
newsitem.headline: Cities moving to ban tobacco billboards.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

The Supreme Court's action allowing Baltimore's ban of tobacco billboard advertising near places where children gather is encouraging lawmakers in other cities including New York to seek similar restrictions.

On Wednesday, New York City Council Speaker Peter Vallone introduced legislation banning cigarette and smokeless tobacco advertising and promotion within 1,000 feet of playgrounds, schools, child day care centers, children's institutions and youth amusement arcades.
New York is the largest city to seek such restrictions and similar moves are now considered in other cities including Washington, D.C. and Seattle.

In the Seattle area, the King County Board of Health is scheduled to vote on May 30 on a proposal to ban tobacco billboard advertising within 1,000 feet of schools and other places where children gather.
The board is expected to vote later on related measures that would include regulation of the placement of tobacco items in stores where minors shop.

Meanwhile, a bill is expected to be introduced soon before the Washington, D.C. city council that would ban tobacco billboards within 2,000 feet of schools and other areas frequented by children. The bill is to contain other restrictions on advertising and marketing tobacco products.
Baltimore, Cincinnati and Long Beach, Calif., are among cities that have previously passed legislation restricting tobacco billboard advertising.

Anti-smoking forces predict the number of cities seeking similar laws will increase after Monday's action by the Supreme Court to reject a constitutional free-speech challenge to Baltimore's ban, which also applies to liquor ads.
"This is going to have a catalyst effect, a snowballing effect," said William Novelli, president of the Washington-based Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids.

The high court's action involving the Baltimore ban came just three days after a federal judge in North Carolina ruled the Food and Drug Administration could regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes, but had no authority over advertising.

The decision to let the Baltimore ban stand came without comment or dissent from the justices and does not create a nationwide precedent. But legal experts said the move could be viewed as support for governmental authority to limit ads that might reach children.

George Dessart, chairman of the American Cancer Society, told a news conference in Manhattan that he expected the New York City proposal would further embolden politicians in other jurisdictions to move forward.
Novelli agreed.
"I think when New York City takes on an issue, people stand up and take notice," he said in a telephone interview.
Both New York City and New York State are among governments that have sued the tobacco industry to recoup health costs of treating smokers.

Novelli said that Dan Jaffe of the Association of National Advertisers was quoted in published reports following the Supreme Court ruling as saying that his industry would challenge any other cities that passed such restrictions.
Jaffe was quoted as saying such moves would be a "very expensive mistake."
Novelli said while Jaffe appeared to be laying down the gauntlet, the New York City proposal would give support to other lawmakers.
"It sends a message to other cities that there is not much to fear," he said.
Novelli said that his group will help these efforts by providing material to other cities and municipalities that want to pass similar laws.

In addition to banning billboards near schools, the New York proposal would prohibit the sale or distribution of hats, T-shirts and other promotional items with domestic tobacco brand names within 1,000 feet of schools and other places where children gather.
